newsitem.title: CHINA: China urban growth seen spurring soybean imports.
newsitem.headline: China urban growth seen spurring soybean imports.

text.p: More than half a billion Chinese will be living in cities by 2005, helping to push annual soybean imports to 12 million tonnes, from 1.7 million in 1996, a U.S. official said on Wednesday.

China's population is forecast to reach 1.34 billion in 2005, up from the current 1.2 billion, with 536 million people living in urban areas, up from the current 343 million, Doug Magnus, of the United Soybean Board (USB), said.

The number of Chinese living in the countryside would fall to 804 million, from the current 855 million, as people continue to move to the cities in search of work, he told a conference on China's Oils/Fats and Feed Ingredients Markets '97 organised by Singapore's Centre for Management Technology.

Increased demand for meat as incomes rise with economic growth, seen at about 10 percent a year, would mean China would need to import 12 million tonnes of soybeans a year, said Magnus, who chairs the USB's international marketing committee.
China imported 1.7 million tonnes of soybeans in 1996, he said, and so far in 1997 had bought more than 1.5 million tonnes of soybeans on the world market.
Asian traders reported further soybean purchases on the world market earlier this week of at least 200,000 tonnes, which would put total 1997 imports at more than 1.7 million.

China had already turned from being an exporter of soybeans in 1994 when it sold 8.27 million tonnes, Magnus said. The same situation appliced to soybean meal, with exports of 1.3 million tonnes in 1984 compared with 2.7 million tonnes of imports in 1996, he said.
These imports had been spurred by a rise in poultry consumption, which hit 11 million tonnes in 1996, up from 8.2 million tonnes in 1995, and 1.85 million tonnnes in 1985.
Pork production was also soaring, Magnus said, hitting 37 million tonnes in 1996, up from 36 million tonnes in 1995, 18 million tonnes in 1987 and seven million tonnes in 1975.
China had seven times the number of hogs compared with the United States but produced only 4.5 times as much pork, he said.
Increased efficiency in pork production would be a major factor behind rises in demand for soybean meal, which is used to make animal feed, Magnus said.
